tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

schema.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
schema.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

schema.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
schema.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. ## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

Return bounded page-located evidence, label external fallback sources explicitly, and never represent a Reference Stub as a reviewed Paper Brief. ---
type: video-summary
video_id: Bel_U51k71Y
title: "SSAC16: Sport Science: Extending the Athlete's Peak Performance"
event: SSAC16 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Brian cop (caption spelling), Eric Corum (caption spelling), St Smith (caption spelling; addressed as Stephen), Dr David Martin, chrisy ashwan (caption spelling), Tom har harro (caption spelling)]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, basketball, american-football, decision-making, other-sport:cycling, other-sport:rugby]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A moderated panel (presented by Catapult) of a football high performance coach, a 76ers research head, a rugby and Australian sport veteran, a science writer and a Catapult executive. The theme is that sport science fails when it ignores people: buy-in, trust and culture matter more than any single metric. Panelists argue for individualized load, recovery as part of adaptation, caution against over-reading risk data and against pulling athletes back, and tying measures to performance outcomes players care about. The close covers nutrition monitoring, doping incentives and whether players trust wearables.

## Key claims

- Poor results are usually a mismatch between the scientist and the coach and athlete, and sport science should not be judged by a team's win-loss record. [02:32] [03:02]
- A rugby culture reset had the team write the articles they wanted written about them. [04:34] [05:06]
- At a football program, buy-in follows winning and meeting a need; it is a service role. [06:36] [07:37]
- Do not import "what worked here"; learn the culture before offering solutions. [08:08]
- The "sports science" label can read as a lab and be unwelcome; blame follows losses and credit goes to the people involved. [08:39] [09:40]
- Belief in the support staff builds team confidence; Australian resource limits spurred innovation. [10:10] [11:10] [11:42]
- Scientists should question assumed answers and fit into the existing culture. [12:43]
- Recovery is part of adaptation, and athletes differ in how they recover. [14:14] [14:44] [15:14]
- Data and talking to the athlete both matter; no single recovery number exists, and asking the athlete is the best current tool if they are paying attention. [15:46] [16:47]
- Without trust, athletes may say they feel fine to stay in the game. [17:19]
- Coaches can confuse talent and readiness; a talented freshman may lack work capacity. [18:20]
- A fluid plan that adjusts dose up or down by the athlete's daily state is reported to beat a static plan. [19:20] [19:51]
- Sport science has gone too far toward rest; every pull-back limits overload, so respond to modifiable risk factors by changing training. [20:22] [20:52] [21:22]
- Monitoring something not understood can create self-fulfilling beliefs; the panelist describes a fetal monitoring example and sleep feedback studies. [22:22] [22:52] [23:23]
- Published thresholds do not hold for real athletes; ask a performance question, collect broad data, then see what it says. [23:54] [24:24]
- An NBA coach wanted to know "where the cliff is" to push to the edge safely. [24:54]
- Smart periodization allows harder camps with more players ready. [25:24]
- NCAA rules limiting football in practice, and acclimatization rules, are criticized as counterproductive. [25:56] [26:26] [26:57]
- All stress counts, including academic and social. [27:59] [28:29]
- A one-week sleep change (no console after 10) was followed by a higher game grade for one player. [29:31] [30:03]
- The relationship between practitioner and athlete may matter more than the method. [30:33] [31:05]
- Black-box monitoring breeds suspicion; feed results back to players. [32:38] [33:08]
- Policing athletes with devices backfires. [34:10]
- Skill sports allow more leniency than cycling, and NBA travel stress is gaining recognition. [35:44] [36:15] [37:17]
- A poster of NBA injuries found game days and back-to-backs weakly predictive; usage was better; practice time is also missing. [37:49] [38:19] [38:50]
- Injuries persist because people seek a silver bullet; measure athlete response across several types of data. [39:50] [40:21] [40:51]
- A well-designed physical preparation program and training plan come first. [42:25] [42:55]
- Athletes want what they like, not what they need; evidence points to food, sleep and consistent training. [43:26]
- Motivational interviewing lets the athlete drive the conversation. [45:28] [45:59]
- Sit beside coaches and wait to be asked; people usually reject the scientist, not the science. [46:29] [47:00] [47:30] [48:01]
- Link a measure to a performance marker to earn buy-in, but watch for exceptions. [48:01] [48:31] [49:03]

## Numbers and definitions

- Philadelphia 76ers: "eight wins" (caption; Van Gundy quip). [01:02]
- Australia: panelist spent 21 years there. [09:40]
- Rowing study: 350 rowers; two chosen; a gold medal eight years later (place caption "camber area"). [12:43]
- Jimmy Butler: 38 or 39 minutes cited as the moderator's example. [15:14]
- Fluid periodization: adjust up 20 to 25% over plan on good days; "150 to like 500%" more improvement versus a static model on the same rack and position; panelist says it is published or will be, with a dissertation online. [19:20] [19:51]
- Sleep feedback studies: groups of "two 300 people"; told sleep architecture was about two standard deviations below normal; cognitive impairment after three to five days. [22:22] [22:52]
- Fetal heart monitoring: almost a decade of more cesarean births. [22:22]
- Game grade: from the 70s to 86% to the 90s; sleep four and a half hours a night; lost the first game. [29:01] [29:31] [30:03]
- Free-throw drill: 1,000 free throws per group of three after two hours of sleep. [44:26]
- Nutrition scale: 120 players, 85 scholarship. [53:07]
- Cyclist diet reporting: about three weeks to build reporting confidence. [55:42]
- Weight fines: 10 grand for four pounds as a hypothetical. [57:15]
- Poster: two years, 500 injuries (caption "I think two years... 500 injuries"). [37:49]
- Back-to-back and playing-day predictability is described as limited. [38:19]
- Garbled: "Al Duz is a 35 minute sufferfest" (caption). [35:44]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Fluid periodization: planned load adjusted daily by athlete state, with players choosing monitoring tools. [19:20] [19:51]
- Training-recovery-adaptation cycle (super-compensation style description). [14:14] [14:44]
- Baseline plus subjective feel plus wearable data (HRV, morning heart rate named). [15:46] [16:47]
- General Adaptation Syndrome for total stress. [28:29]
- Motivational interviewing. [45:28]
- Tie a measure to a performance metric and show it before a session. [48:01] [48:31]
- Energy balance by power meters, body composition and metabolic rate for cyclists. [55:42] [56:13]
- Pre-plated meals for NBA weight loss. [56:13]

## Limits and open questions

- Mostly experience and anecdote; speakers are partly vendors and staff with interests (a Catapult-presented panel). [00:00]
- The fluid-periodization figures are recalled from a dissertation, not shown. [19:51]
- The sleep story is one player in one week and the team lost. [29:31] [30:03]
- The injury poster is described as limited by its authors and the panelist. [38:19]
- Panel contradicts itself on measurement: no single number captures recovery, yet panelists describe tying a number to outcomes. [16:47] [48:31]
- Speaker attribution is inferred from the moderator's addresses; names are caption garbled.

## Q&A

- Reinjury risk for an unusual case (the moderator's example is the 76ers center): small data, so crowdsource experts, take a cautious path without consensus, and use only unanimous believers. [50:04] [50:34] [51:06] [52:37]
- Measuring nutrition: hard at 120 players; change the training table and educate first; self-reports were distorted in a cyclist study; use energy balance where possible. [52:37] [53:07] [54:39] [55:10]
- NBA weight loss: pre-plating, and weight fines as a mixed motivator. [56:13] [56:43] [57:15]
- Doping: incentives and weak regulation drive it more than technology; tracking data could flag anomalies. [57:15] [57:45] [59:48]
- Do players see tracking as an enemy: use in a vacuum breeds distrust; explaining it builds acceptance. [1:00:20] [1:01:20] [1:01:50]

# Applications: Sport science, extending the athlete's peak performance

## Where this applies

- Inference: Tie one monitored variable to a performance outcome the coaches already care about, and show it in one slide at the start of a session. A panelist did this by linking team sleep totals to passing accuracy [48:31]; at Baylor the pair could be sleep or mRSI against a practice efficiency or PFF-graded measure, shown to the position group.
- Inference: Try a "fluid" week for a small group: keep the planned load but let the player's daily readiness shift the dose up as well as down. The Kentucky example adjusted by 20 to 25% above plan on good days [19:51]. At Baylor this means a rule in the plan, agreed with the strength coach, for when the day goes up.
- Inference: Reframe reports to football coaches so "risk flag" always comes with a modifiable factor and a training change, not only a reduction. A panelist argues that pulling athletes back stops overload [21:22].
- Inference: Replace "wear the device or else" with an explanation of what each athlete gets out of it, and ask players for one reason they would opt out. The panel treats being rejected as personal, not about the science [47:30], and warns against policing athletes [34:10].
- Inference: For nutrition at football scale, start with training-table options and education before individual tracking, as the Kentucky coach did with 120 players [53:07].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: "Recovery has to be earned by training hard first," and heavy load monitoring bred a "culture of fear" of under-training (course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The panel agrees strongly: recovery is part of adaptation [14:14], and sport science has gone too far toward pulling athletes back [20:22].
- Eric's baseline: the Applied Performance roster-wide wellness surveys were dropped because athletes learned to game them. The panel agrees on the mechanism, saying athletes may say they feel fine to avoid being benched [17:19], and extends it: trust is the fix, not a new metric.
- Eric's baseline: daily mRSI from CMJ was chosen as the objective readiness marker. The panel conflicts in part: it says the best current tool is asking the athlete, and no single number captures recovery [16:47].
- Eric's baseline: preparedness (long-built capacity) is separate from readiness (day to day) (course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The panel's talent versus readiness point, a freshman with low work capacity [18:20], extends this to coach communication.
- Eric's baseline: an annual plan is a flexible roadmap, and the course teaches undulating periodization (course team position, speaker unconfirmed; the undulating preference is first-person but unattributed). The fluid periodization report [19:51] agrees and adds a daily adjustment rule.
- Eric's baseline: the data dictionary has no position-specific thresholds. The panel's point that published thresholds do not hold for real athletes [23:54] supports building them from Baylor data.
- Eric's baseline: NordBord was dropped for 120+ athletes because collection could not be sustained. The panel's note that monitoring every player's food at that size is not feasible [53:07] runs parallel.

## What would have to be true

- Enough weeks of consistent data per athlete to show whether a link such as sleep to performance exists in Baylor's group, not only in one cited team.
- Strength and position coaches willing to agree in advance on the upward-adjust rule and who decides.
- A way to record whether a player chose to opt out of a measure, so opt-outs can be tracked without penalty.

## Do not apply when

- Reading the "150 to like 500%" improvement figure as a result. It is a panelist's recall of a dissertation, no sample or design was given [19:51].
- Acting on the sleep story [30:03] as an effect size. It is one player in one week with a game grade, and the speaker lost the game that week.
- Using the belief-effect findings to withhold real sleep or load data from athletes. They argue for care in how results are framed [22:52], not for hiding them.
- Applying the NBA poster finding on back-to-backs [38:19] to football; it is a basketball injury set the speaker calls limited.
- Applying the 76ers or rugby examples when the coach and athlete group are different: a panelist warns against importing "what worked here" [08:08].

## First step

Pick one outcome a football position coach already tracks and one variable Applied Performance already collects, and plot the two for a single position group across last season. Read-only, and show it to that coach before deciding anything.

## Summary

A moderated panel of a current player, a front-office executive, a former player and coach, a WNBA guard and an analytics executive discusses where basketball analytics goes next. The recurring argument is that tracking data is most useful when it produces small, specific, coachable findings (who gets hung up on screens, how often hands go up) and when it reaches players in a form they can use. The panel also covers wearables, tests that players can train for, how to judge coaches, and officiating data. The speakers repeatedly stress that human judgment and communication decide whether a number gets used.

## Key claims

- Camera tracking data is most valuable for small defensive details (screen handling, closeouts, hand position), not for confirming large strategic trends. [02:44]
- Every screen can now be identified and reviewed, which lets analysts speak in coaches' terms. [03:15]
- Giving a coach the percentage of ways an opponent creates a shot lets a staff decide which version to concede. [04:17]
- A panelist argued that a small fix, such as one high hand, can decide a game because runs happen fast. [05:19]
- Data is a way to build a relationship with a player, but it has to be delivered simply; the panel says players are far behind coaches and analysts in understanding numbers. [09:24]
- Seeing percentages about yourself can become a mental problem (a player described being told which direction she shoots better and then overthinking it). [10:25]
- Some panelists said numbers help a team know the opponent better than they help a player know himself. [11:25]
- Some players can take many items and others only one or two, so staff must know the individual. [11:56]
- A panelist told young players they will have to understand analytics eventually, so they should start early. [12:27]
- For acquisitions, the useful question is fit: whether a player's skills overlap with or add to existing players. [19:36]
- A panelist argued against combining skill metrics into one good-or-bad score; instead, keep the skill metrics and weigh them by the team's system. [20:06]
- Fit analysis can be done quickly if the groundwork is built before the deadline. [21:08]
- Psychological or neurological tests should be tested against on-court results before being trusted; vendors who say they can quantify them need checking. [25:12]
- Physical numbers need context: compare a strong, high-jumping player with another who rebounds more. [25:42]
- A team's hand-coordination test matched its deflection chart, but players who trained for the test rose in the rankings without rising in deflections. [28:15]
- Training for a test exclusively changes the result without translating to the game. [28:45]
- Some teams are growing skeptical of wearables and asking whether a device is worth its cost. [29:45]
- One panelist trusts sport scientists by default but wants to confirm they cause no harm and keep looking. [31:16]
- A practice described as a "light" half-court session was tracked as much harder than a full-court one, and the player said this kind of information is crucial. [32:48]
- Perceived exertion compared with tracking data could indicate whether a player is getting hurt, if one player's rating drifts from the group. [33:50]
- A panelist is willing to wear a device in games and argued analytics tools only need to be a little better than what came before, not perfect. [35:21]
- Players who dismiss a mismatch between feel and data are common, and some may use the data as an excuse. [36:53]
- A panelist said team and player interests are nearly always aligned on this data, so the excuse problem is not a reason to withhold it. [37:23]

# Applications: Ball Don't Lie panel (SSAC17)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Limit what each athlete sees from Catapult and VALD to a small, chosen set of items. The panel said some players can take ten items and others one or two [11:56]. At Baylor this means deciding, per position group, which two or three numbers (for example high-speed running exposure or CMJ output) go to the athlete versus staying with the coach.
- Inference: Pair practice effort ratings with tracked load at the athlete level. A panelist described comparing perceived exertion with tracking data and treating a player whose rating drifts from the group as worth a look [33:19]. In football this would be a check of rated effort against Catapult player load for the same session, used as a prompt for a conversation, not a flag.
- Inference: Before a test becomes a decision input, check whether it tracks anything on the field. The panel's example was a hand-coordination test whose scores matched a deflection chart until players trained for the test and their scores rose without the deflections moving [28:15]. The same check applies to any VALD or speed metric Athletic Performance and Applied Performance rely on for readiness or selection.
- Inference: In recruiting and portal evaluation, report skill-level grades side by side instead of one composite, then weigh them against what the Baylor scheme needs. A panelist described stopping at skill metrics and not collapsing them into good or bad [20:06]. PFF position grades could be shown as separate columns per skill.
- Inference: Review practice drills by tracked intensity, not by how the coach labels them. The panel described a drill coaches thought was a throwaway turning out to be tiring when wearables were checked [38:26].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Data collection is judged on cost versus insight, and a test can be valid yet wrong operationally if it cannot be collected consistently (SportSmith pieces, per method-baseline.md). The panel extends this: a panelist argued tools need only be a little better than the status quo, not perfect [35:21]. These are compatible, but the panel says nothing about collection cost.
- Eric's baseline: Daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped after athletes learned to game them, and mRSI from CMJ replaced them for daily readiness. The panel partly conflicts: it treats a player's rating of practice as useful when set against tracking data [33:19], and also notes some players will use the data as an excuse [36:53]. The panel did not report gaming at scale.
- Eric's baseline: The course material says a trained coach's eye is at least as important as technology (marked Inferred, speaker unconfirmed). The panel agrees on the coach side: it says coaches track plays closely in game and the numbers add to that [58:28].

## What would have to be true

- Practice RPE or a similar rating would need to be collected, which Eric's baseline says Baylor stopped for general use. A small trial would need athletes who do not game it.
- Tracking and ratings would need to be time-aligned per session, per athlete, across enough sessions to see a personal pattern (the panel gave no number).
- Any skill-level recruiting view needs a stated scheme fit to compare against, from the coaches.
- Test-the-test needs an on-field outcome measure to check against that Baylor already keeps.

## Do not apply when

- The question is about pro contracts, game-day wearables, or league labor rules; the panel spoke from NBA and WNBA settings (440 NBA players cited [34:21]) and Baylor has college rules and a roster of more than 120 football athletes (per method-baseline.md).
- Sample is small: panel examples were anecdotes from individual players and one front office, with no samples shown.

Pick one recent practice, list the drills by Catapult player load per minute, and show the top and bottom three to the position coach. See whether any drill's rank surprises him. Nothing changes in the plan until he says so.

## Summary

A Major League Baseball league-office official describes the league's response to a spike in Tommy John (UCL reconstruction) surgeries that came to a head in 2014. He lays out four concerns (more surgeries at MLB level, more repeat surgeries, more at youth and high school level, and widespread misperceptions) and the three-part Pitch Smart program built with a medical committee and USA Baseball: pitch count and rest limits, plain-language research, and accurate surgery information. He reports adoption by youth and high school bodies, a leveling off of MLB surgeries, a long-term prospective study, early results on rest-based care and orthobiologics, and new repair and training approaches, stressing that evidence on the newer methods is thin.

## Key claims

- MLB clubs have been required to use a league-wide electronic medical record since 2010, and the league does not share the data publicly until it is ready for peer review; the talk therefore draws on public data [01:09], [01:39].
- The league's 2014 concerns were more MLB surgeries, more second surgeries, more surgery at youth and high school levels, and misperceptions [02:10].
- Disabled list days for the elbow injury hit an all-time high from 2012 to 2014 [02:41].
- MLB surgeries rose and the players were younger, including some of the best young pitchers [03:12], [03:42].
- Players with a second surgery did not come back as strongly as those with a first, in preliminary research [04:12].
- A leading surgeon's practice saw youth and high school patients rise from rare to about a third [04:43].
- Insurance-record studies found the biggest increase in the 15 to 20 age group [05:14].
- A survey found more than half of high school players thought surgery should be done without an injury, and more than half of college players thought velocity rises afterward; the speaker says medical research shows both are wrong [05:46], [06:17].
- The medical committee said youth overuse was the largest factor, and pitching more than 100 innings in a year raised the risk of serious arm injury [07:22], [07:54].
- Pitch Smart, launched in November 2014 with USA Baseball, has three parts: pitch count and rest limits, digestible research, and accurate information [08:54], [09:24], [12:30].
- Adoption: major youth organizations are compliant, and a 2016 national high school federation vote required states to adopt a pitch-based rule [13:03], [13:33], [14:04].
- MLB surgeries have leveled off, and the number of draftees with prior surgery was flat over three years after a record in 2016 [14:36], [15:06], [15:37].
- A long-term study enrolls drafted players with MRI, biomechanics and history, and follows them through the medical record [16:08], [16:39].

- A team study found most players with partial tears returned after six to eight weeks of rest without surgery; a second found tear location mattered [18:13], [18:43], [19:14].

# Applications: Avoiding Tommy John

## Where this applies

- Inference: Intake data for incoming athletes. The league's long-term study starts at draft with MRI, a biomechanical evaluation, and a playing-history questionnaire, then follows each player through the electronic medical record [16:08], [16:39]. Baylor could keep a smaller version: at arrival, store VALD baselines plus a short history of prior workload and injuries for each athlete, so later injuries can be compared with something recorded before them.
- Inference: Return-to-play decisions after a partial injury. The speaker cited a team study where rest alone brought most partial UCL tear players back without surgery [18:13], and a second study where tear location mattered [19:14]. For football soft tissue or joint injuries, Athletic Medicine could ask whether a defined rest window before testing is reasonable, and what Applied Performance testing would show at the end of it. This is a question for Athletic Medicine, not a recommendation.
- Inference: Cautious handling of new recovery products. The speaker said PRP and stem cells had little peer-reviewed support over rest and rehab alone, and that it was unclear whether rest or the injection explained recoveries [20:14], [21:16]. Before Baylor adopts a new recovery or rehab technology, require a comparison against rest or the current protocol.
- Inference: Reporting overuse in a way staff can act on. The talk shows policy driven by clear thresholds with stated rest rules [09:24]. Applied Performance could write the equivalent for baseball and softball throwing volume if those teams are in scope.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through progression of load and collaboration with Athletic Medicine (course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The talk agrees: the speaker said injuries can be reduced but never eradicated [29:22].
- Eric's baseline: Abrupt, large changes in volume and intensity are treated as an injury-risk driver (course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The talk extends this: the pitch count and rest rules are one way of limiting abrupt exposure [09:24].
- Eric's baseline: NordBord testing is kept for small groups with a clear clinical purpose and dedicated oversight, and dropped where collection cannot be consistent. The talk shows a comparable pattern at league level: the long-term study works because the medical record removes follow-up burden [16:39].
- Eric's baseline: No formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric. The talk is preliminary on risk factors too and says actionable results are some time away [17:42].

## What would have to be true

- Baylor would need to follow athletes long enough for injuries to occur and be recorded in a consistent record. The league study depends on a system all clubs must use [01:09].
- A rest-before-surgery idea needs Athletic Medicine's own caseload. The cited samples were small (43 players in the first study [18:43]), and the speaker himself said conclusions were hard to draw.
- Any workload threshold needs Baylor's own exposure data. Football throws and baseball pitches are not interchangeable.

## Do not apply when

- The population is football. The talk is about throwing injuries in pitchers. The risk factors it names (fastball usage, velocity, innings, rest [17:42]) have no football equivalent that can be borrowed.
- The pitch-count tables are treated as evidence of effectiveness. The speaker said the number of surgeries leveled off but did not claim the guidelines caused that [14:36], [15:37].
- A treatment is judged on a single anecdote or on 43 players.
- The talk is read as independent. The speaker is an MLB league-office official describing the league's own program, and he described unpublished league data as not shared publicly [01:09].

Draft a one-page list of the baseline measures and history items Baylor already records for each football athlete at entry, and mark which ones would be needed to look back at a later injury. Do not add new collection yet.

## Summary

A sports cardiologist argues that endurance athletes stall when they train in a narrow band of heart rate right around their ventilatory threshold, which he calls the physiologic doldrums. He says the fix is to combine laboratory measurements (measured max heart rate, oxygen uptake, and threshold) with the athlete's own field data, then split training into clearly easy and clearly hard work. He illustrates this with one 26-year-old elite rower who trained 13 sessions a week, clustered at threshold, and improved his threshold heart rate over about eleven months while training less. The talk matters because it challenges formula-based heart-rate zones and flat zone charts on consumer devices. The evidence is one case plus the speaker's program experience.

## Key claims

- Performance work rests on basic exercise physiology, and athletes differ, so each one has to be measured and re-measured [01:33].
- Lab physiology without field analytics, or the reverse, leads to the doldrums [02:03].
- Roughly 40% of athletic adults over 40 in one local study felt dismissed by their doctors because they were athletes [03:35].
- About half of elite athletes who arrive with a performance decline have an undetected medical cause (the speaker notes selection bias), so medical causes should be ruled out first [07:38].
- Oxygen flows lung to heart and circulation to muscle, and all three links are trainable (the speaker hints lungs are not the one that changed here) [09:10].
- Heart rate, oxygen uptake and work rate are linear in a healthy person, while carbon dioxide output steepens above a point called the ventilatory threshold [10:10].
- That threshold is, in his view, the single most important measurement for elite athletes, and physiologically there are only two zones, below it (sustainable for hours with fuel and fluids) and above it (effort-dependent fatigue) [10:40] [11:10].
- Equations for max heart rate are unreliable and should be replaced by measurement [11:40].
- Easy days must sit clearly below the threshold and hard days clearly above it, with little to gain in between [17:17] [17:47].
- Coaches who apply physiology tend to win and those who ignore it lose, in his experience [18:48].
- A reassessment cycle in the lab, about every four months in this case, keeps the plan honest [19:19].
- Heart rate variability is a fickle measure and he has not seen it work alone at the elite level, though he accepts it as a backup to subjective recovery [22:54].
- Changes in the power-to-heart-rate relationship are the best sign of fitness change for athletes with power meters [25:26].
- The lab fits endurance-heavy athletes best, because anaerobic lab tests such as the Wingate engage different machinery from the sport [26:27].

## Numbers and definitions

- Max heart rate prediction error: the true standard deviation is on the order of 15 to 20 beats per minute [12:11].
- Case athlete at baseline: measured max heart rate 208, peak oxygen uptake 71 mL per kg, threshold at 78% of max oxygen uptake at a heart rate of about 162 [12:41].
- Tracking period requested before any change: 90 days [13:11].
- Training before intervention: 13 sessions per week, about 18 hours, 11 base-building and 2 higher-intensity [13:41].
- Field heart rate: base sessions about 160 plus or minus 2, hard sessions about 12 beats higher, resting about 52, felt recovered 50% of the time [14:12]. Caption at [15:14] gives 180 and 172 for these sessions, which conflicts with 160 and +12; probably garbled.
- Doldrums: roughly 5 beats above and 5 below the threshold heart rate [16:46].
- Goal horizon: an 18-month periodized plan toward an Olympic team [18:18].
- Reassessment every four months, and the third reassessment came roughly eleven months later [19:19].
- After the program: threshold heart rate 162 to 176 (a 10 to 15% rise), peak heart rate unchanged, peak oxygen uptake only slightly higher [19:49].
- Field after: base heart rates in the 150s, hard intervals close to 180, resting heart rate lower [20:20]; felt recovered 70% of the time, up from 50% [20:51].
- Hard-interval average 179 with a standard deviation of 8 to 10 beats (caption wording unclear about which) [24:40].
- Subjective measure: a 1 to 10 satisfaction score for each workout [13:41].
- Context: program started in 2007 [05:05]; only one quarter of the studied masters athletes were risk-factor free [03:35].

## Methods and frameworks named

- A four-step sequence for suboptimal performance: medical evaluation, physiology evaluation, training evaluation, then planning, reassessment and implementation [07:07].
- Lab measures: max heart rate, aerobic efficiency (slope of oxygen against work), ventilatory threshold [12:11].
- Field data: 90 days of untouched training with a heart-rate monitor and a satisfaction rating [13:41].
- Training plan: individualize physiology, set a calendar working back from the goal event, assess the support structure (coach, nutrition, family), and run a longitudinal reassessment loop [16:46] [18:18].
- Sub-doldrum sessions are aerobic base, technique and active recovery. Supra-doldrum sessions include steady state, short and long intervals [17:17] [17:47].

## Limits and open questions

- One athlete, no control and no group data. Other changes during the eleven months are not shown.
- The speaker states his program has financial relationships with local and national groups (disclosed at [01:02]).
- Some figures are hard to verify due to captions (see Numbers).
- The oxygen-uptake threshold is described as "the single most important measurement" without data beyond the case.
- Heart rate variability skepticism is opinion, no data shown.
- Whether the same split works in team sports is not shown; he says the lab suits endurance components [26:27].

## Q&A

- Heart rate variability: promising in theory, many confounders, useful only as a backup to how the athlete feels [22:23] [22:54].
- Did the volume drop explain the gain: no, the key change was two clearly different kinds of days [23:33].
- Race-day intensity and the variance in hard sessions: hard sessions varied in effort to mimic race conditions, and he says most athletes improve when forced to rest after injury [24:10] [24:40].
- Power meters: pair power with heart rate, a rise in power at a given heart rate signals adaptation [25:26].
- Anaerobic power testing: Wingate is limited, better to use the sport's own exercises as benchmarks [25:56] [26:27].

# Applications for Baylor Applied Performance

## Where this applies

- Inference: Replace any age-based or percentage-of-predicted heart rate zones used for conditioning with a measured max heart rate and a measured threshold heart rate for each athlete who runs aerobic work (football conditioning tests, Olympic-sport endurance athletes). The speaker calls prediction equations unreliable with a spread of 15 to 20 bpm [12:11], so any zone table that starts from a formula is the first thing to check.
- Inference: Audit aerobic "base" days in GPS and heart-rate exports for a pile-up near one intensity. The talk's rower did base and hard sessions within a few beats of his threshold [15:45]. Catapult heart-rate band time per session would show whether a sport group clusters in the middle.
- Inference: For return-to-performance athletes and endurance-heavy sport groups, adopt a repeating reassessment cycle (the speaker used every four months [19:19]) and pair lab-style threshold data with what the athlete does in the field.
- Inference: Add a one-question 1 to 10 satisfaction rating per session for a small pilot group, read next to heart-rate data, to see whether easy days feel too satisfying and hard days too unsatisfying, as in the case shown [14:43].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: conditioning zones are assigned by athlete body size (about 165, 170, 175 bpm anaerobic threshold for big, medium, small), and a nearby slide also shows an age formula (220 minus age) without saying which is used in practice [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29; Tension 6]. The talk extends and partly conflicts: it rejects any formula-based max and says to measure it [12:11]. It does not endorse a body-size lookup either.
- Eric's baseline: intensities in roughly the 75 to 90% band are labelled "no man's land" and avoided as a primary target [class-4-2026.md p.48]. The talk agrees in spirit with its "doldrums" band of about 5 beats either side of threshold [17:17], but defines the band by threshold heart rate, not percent of max effort.
- Eric's baseline: aerobic training is kept below anaerobic threshold with a work-to-rest ratio of 1:1 to 1:2 [week3-lecture.md p.51]. The talk agrees that low-intensity days belong clearly below threshold [17:47].
- Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped for the general roster because athletes learned to game them, but kept for return-to-play [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]. The talk's rating is a session-satisfaction score on a rower with a 90-day tracking period, a different use. It does not resolve the gaming problem.
- Eric's baseline: preparedness is separated from day-to-day readiness (course team position, speaker unconfirmed) [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]. The talk treats threshold heart rate as the best gauge of training response [19:49], which fits preparedness, and treats heart rate variability as unreliable alone [22:54].
- Eric's baseline: testing must be repeated exactly the same way over time or comparisons fail (course team position, speaker unconfirmed) [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6]. The talk agrees by reassessing in the same lab on a fixed schedule [19:19].

## What would have to be true

- Access to metabolic or gas-exchange testing, or an equivalent threshold test, which the speaker's lab method relies on [10:40]. Without it, the threshold-based zones cannot be set the way he describes.
- A heart-rate monitor on the athlete in every session for at least a baseline tracking period (he asks for 90 days [13:11]).
- A sport where steady-state endurance work matters. The speaker says the lab suits team athletes only where there is an endurance component [26:27].
- Enough athletes in a comparable group to see whether the clustering pattern is common or unique to one person.

## Do not apply when

- The sport is power or speed dominated (most football positions): the speaker says the lab is of limited value for anaerobic power and that the actual exercises are better benchmarks [26:27].
- The only evidence is the single rower case. It is one 26-year-old athlete [06:37] and the speaker calls it one of many examples, with no group data shown. No control comparison, so the improvement could include other changes.
- Heart-rate data is poor quality (strap dropout, chest strap not worn). Heart rate can drift with heat, caffeine and fatigue, so a threshold heart rate fixed from one test can go stale. This is an Inference, not stated in the talk.
- The aim is a daily readiness decision from heart rate variability: the speaker did not endorse that [22:54].

## First step

Pick one endurance-oriented group (for example a cross-country or rowing-type athlete, or a football conditioning test group). Export two weeks of session heart-rate band time from Catapult and check whether most easy and hard sessions sit within about 10 beats of each other. No change to training, just a look.

## Summary

A panel of a players' association researcher, a sports technology adviser, a former NFL player with a neck injury and an anatomist discusses why sports science has not made injuries disappear. The panel stresses trust, communication and athlete access to their own data over technology alone. They discuss the tension between player health and contract risk, the role of independent medical opinions, personalized protection and care, and why adoption of sports science varies. It is a discussion of practice and culture, with one personal injury account, and offers no data analysis.

## Key claims

- Football's anatomy (head leaning forward, weak neck) means higher injury risk by sport design. [02:02, 02:35]
- Team doctors work for the team, so concussions may not reach independent care; a panelist wants doctors inside locker rooms. [03:07, 03:37]
- Communication and trust are the most integral part of a program. [04:09, 05:09]
- Technology is an enabler; experts must give context and explain to athletes why they are doing it. [05:40, 06:10]
- The aim is to mitigate risk, not eliminate injuries; in key games the best players still play. [06:10, 06:40]
- Next steps for data are sport, then position, then individual context. [08:11, 08:42]
- One player says a daily check on sleep and eating, with a readiness percentage, helped him. [09:45, 10:16]
- A wearables committee was set up under the latest collective bargaining agreement to vet products for reliability and validity, with privacy and legal layers. [11:18]
- A new ligament in the front of the neck has been described recently. [12:24]
- The player describes a neck fracture and spinal cord contusion; he says he does not know if it was preventable. [13:56, 16:32, 21:09]
- The panel says the mental side of injury is large, and the union finds former players with similar injuries to talk to current players. [22:44, 23:14]
- A retired-player health screening program and research on retirees are in place. [24:18, 24:48]
- Parties in an injury (GM, medical director, athlete, agent, owner) need different framing. [26:21]
- Open organizations without silos tend to do best, as seen by one panelist. [27:23, 28:24]
- Athletes may not be honest about sleep or soreness if they fear consequences, and injury history affects contracts. [30:30, 31:01, 32:04]
- Giving athletes more medical options and giving both parties access to the same data may help. [33:07, 34:09]
- Athletes are treated too similarly; a panelist wants personalized imaging and equipment. [35:11, 36:12]
- Meals at team facilities are now standard, unlike in 2005. [38:18, 38:49]
- Sports science took longer to take hold in the US for reasons including athlete numbers abroad, framing of the tool to coaches, and strong unions. [40:24, 40:54, 42:28]
- Teams now add performance staff instead of handing technology to a strength coach. [41:56]

## Numbers and definitions

- Head about "five kilos." [02:02]
- Player injury date given as "November 1st 2015." [13:56]
- Readiness percentages of 70% and 90% in the daily check. [10:16]
- A caption about a speed of "25 and 1/2 miles per hour" for a player is garbled. [07:10]
- A book of anatomical variation of "almost 2,000 pages." [35:42]
- DNA sequencing "in 15 minutes." [12:54]
- Training instruction examples of 50%, 60%, 80% and 100% effort. [36:44]
- "Handful" of teams provided breakfast in 2005, among thirty. [38:18]
- A head to toe imaging session estimated at "a couple of hours." [42:59]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Daily readiness check from sleep and nutrition information. [09:45]
- Wearables vetting committee. [11:18]
- Personalized imaging and equipment fit. [36:12]
- Access to collected data for both sides. [34:09]

## Limits and open questions

- No data, sample or study is shown.
- Captions have no speaker labels; attributions are inferred from context and the introduction.
- The injury story is one case; the player says he cannot tell if it could have been prevented.
- One panelist works for a technology company; his claims about technology practice are an institutional view.
- Nutrition remarks are opinion.
- Names of staff in the Seattle story are garbled.

## Q&A

- Advancements in nutrition. [37:16]
- Why some teams and leagues are less receptive to new data. [39:22]
- Whether detailed imaging per athlete is realistic. [42:28]

# Applications: SSAC18 Risky Business Sports Science and Injury Prevention

## Where this applies

- Inference: Explaining monitoring output to football players. The technology-company panelist says the best teams explain why a device is worn and show the output [05:40, 06:10]. This is a concrete step for how GPS and force-plate results are presented in position meetings.
- Inference: Athlete access to their own data. The panel describes both sides receiving the same information from wearables [34:09]. Baylor could define what a player sees from GPS and VALD and when, so the data does not feel one-way.
- Inference: Handling the pressure not to report soreness. A player describes the contract and playing-time cost of admitting a problem [31:01, 32:04]. For Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine, this argues for a routine in which self-report is kept separate from selection decisions.
- Inference: Position-specific context for load. The panel says the next step after sport-level context is position and individual context, with receivers and cornerbacks as the example [08:11]. This fits splitting GPS thresholds by position group rather than team-wide.
- Inference: Communication across parties after an injury (coach, medical director, player, agent) [26:21]. A short template for what each party gets could be drafted with Athletic Medicine.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine (Inferred, course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The panel's "mitigate risk" framing [06:10] agrees.
- Eric's baseline: daily wellness surveys were dropped for the roster after about a year because athletes learned to game them, but are kept for return to play and chronic conditions. A panelist describes a daily readiness check built on sleep and eating habits as valuable to him [09:45, 10:16]. This conflicts for general use and agrees with keeping subjective data in individual cases. The panelist also says honesty depends on no punishment for honest answers [30:30].
- Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's stated role is to supply information that supports decisions by Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine. The panel's "technology is an enabler, experts interpret" [05:40] agrees.
- Eric's baseline: no recovery, sleep or formal injury-risk protocol is attributed to Eric in the corpus. The panel does not supply one either.

## What would have to be true

- A clear policy on who sees what data, agreed with Athletic Medicine and the compliance office, before extending athlete access.
- Buy-in from position coaches, who the panel says need tools framed inside their own approach [40:54].
- Enough athletes per position group for any position-level split to be meaningful.

## Do not apply when

- The ideas come from pro union and league settings (collective bargaining agreement committee on wearables [11:18], contract effects of injury history [31:01]). College athletes have a different structure and no equivalent contract pressure.
- A single player's story (the neck injury [13:56]) is treated as a basis for a program-wide protocol. The panelist himself says he does not know if it was preventable [16:32].
- Imaging each athlete head to toe [42:59] is proposed without a medical owner, cost and consent plan. This was a panelist's idea, not a described program.
- Nutrition remarks [37:16] are used as evidence. They are opinion and anecdote.

## First step

Draft a one-page "what the athlete sees" note for one monitoring tool (for example GPS summary after a game), then review it with Athletic Medicine before showing it to anyone else.

**Scope:** I checked 5 videos: about 70 summary claims against the transcript text at their locators, and every "Eric's baseline:" line against method-baseline.md. All locators I tested exist. I found no invented numbers or Baylor specifics in the summaries.

### Bel_U51k71Y: PASS WITH FIXES
1. **applications.md, Eric's baseline, wellness bullet.** The doc says the panel "agrees on the mechanism" [17:19]. The baseline (line 71) says surveys failed because athletes gave "consistent, low-effort answers". The panelist [17:19] describes strategic lying to avoid being benched. These are different mechanisms. Replace with: "The panel names a different failure: athletes may say they feel fine to stay in the lineup [17:19]. Eric's baseline describes low-effort sameness. Both point to trust as the fix."
2. **applications.md, mRSI bullet.** The doc says "The panel conflicts in part: ... the best current tool is asking the athlete" [16:47]. The transcript continues: "but you can't just do that", and says tracking tools help teach athletes patterns (HRV and morning heart rate are named). Replace "conflicts in part" with: "Partly agrees: the panelist treats numbers as a teaching aid alongside self-report, not a single readiness score [16:47]."
3. Confidence `untested` is correct for this panel.

### 81CC-uLrOtE: PASS WITH FIXES
1. **summary.md, frontmatter.** `confidence: supported`, but the summary's own Limits section says "Most evidence is anecdote; no sample sizes or results". Under the brief's ceiling this must be `untested`.
2. **summary.md, key claim [32:48].** The doc says the practice "was tracked as much harder than a full-court one". The source [32:17] is a player's hypothetical: a coach calls it "an easy day... half court... then that practice is 10 times harder", followed by "from what I understand... Zephyr can track that". Nothing was tracked. Replace with: "A player argued that a supposedly easy half-court practice can be far harder ('10 times', his estimate) than a full-court one, and that wearables could show this [32:17] [32:48]."
3. **applications.md, Eric's baseline, coach's-eye bullet.** "the numbers add to that [58:28]": the transcript at [58:28] only praises coaches' recall and bench-computer tracking. Delete "and the numbers add to that".
4. **applications.md, Where this applies, bullet 2.** "A panelist described comparing perceived exertion..." [33:19]: the speaker is reporting what some team does ("they're using that"). Replace "A panelist described" with "A panelist reported a team that compares".

### sHXuxj3-rbQ: PASS WITH FIXES
1. **summary.md, key claim [15:37].** The doc says draftee surgeries were "flat over three years after a record in 2016". The source says they "set an all-time high in 2016 but... relatively flat over the last three year period". The record falls inside the flat period, not before it. Replace with: "flat over the last three years, with 2016 itself a record high".
2. **summary.md, key claim [07:54].** "more than 100 innings": the source says "100 or more" (the Numbers section has it right). Fix the key claim to match.
3. **summary.md, Q&A [31:54].** The speaker says yearly rest "has been proven to reduce injuries" but names no study. Add: "(no study named)".
4. **applications.md, NordBord bullet.** "the long-term study works because the medical record removes follow-up burden [16:39]": the study is still enrolling and has no results, so "works" is unsupported, and the line is unlabeled. Replace with: "Inference: the study is designed to avoid dropout by using the medical record [16:39]; results are not yet reported."
5. Confidence `supported` is defensible because published studies are cited. Note in the summary that the source is an institutional self-report.

### JuUBObeNGfc: PASS WITH FIXES (closest to FAIL)
1. **summary.md, frontmatter.** `confidence: supported` for a single case ("one athlete, no control", per its own Limits section) from a clinic with disclosed financial ties [01:02]. The brief says `untested` for single cases. Change it.
2. **summary.md, Numbers [19:49].** "threshold heart rate 162 to 176 (a 10 to 15% rise)": 162 to 176 is about 8.6%. The speaker said "10 or 15%". Record both: "162 to 176 (about 9% by arithmetic; the speaker said '10 or 15%')".
3. **applications.md, preparedness bullet.** "...best gauge of training response [19:49], which fits preparedness": that last clause is the writer's reasoning, unlabeled. Make it "Inference: this fits preparedness."
